steps.say: A painless lump exactly in the middle of a toddler's neck, sitting at or just below the small U-shaped bone under the chin, is a thyroglossal cyst until proved otherwise. The swelling comes from a leftover channel of the thyroid's journey down from the tongue, and it often bobs upward when the child swallows or sticks the tongue out.
steps.tx: An upper **midline cyst** (central neck lump) in a toddler is a **thyroglossal duct cyst** (thyroid descent remnant) until proved otherwise. It arises at the **foramen cecum** (tongue base pit) and usually presents at or just below the **hyoid bone** (U-shaped neck bone), often rising with swallowing or tongue protrusion.

steps.say: The thyroid starts at the back of the tongue and travels down the neck before birth, trailing a thin channel behind it. Sometimes a piece never makes the journey and stays at the tongue base as a lingual thyroid. That lump may be the child's only working thyroid tissue.
steps.tx: The thyroid descends from the **foramen cecum** (tongue pit) attached by the **thyroglossal duct** (descent channel). Failed caudal migration leaves a **lingual thyroid** (tongue-base gland) with no other thyroid tissue in the neck, recognised on imaging before any midline surgery is planned.

steps.say: Before any knife touches a midline neck lump, confirm there is a normal thyroid sitting lower in the neck. A simple sound-wave scan or tracer scan maps the gland, guiding safe surgery. Removing the only functioning thyroid by mistake condemns the child to lifelong hormone tablets. No lower gland with a tongue lump means the lump is the whole thyroid, so surgery stops.
steps.tx: **Ultrasound** (sound-wave scan) or **radionuclide imaging** (tracer scan) identifies **ectopic thyroid** (misplaced gland tissue) before midline neck surgery. Demonstrating a normal lower gland protects the only functioning thyroid from accidental removal and lifelong **hypothyroidism** (thyroid failure). An absent lower gland with a tongue-base lump means **ectopic thyroid** (only tissue), and surgery is cancelled.

steps.say: The standard operation removes the whole channel, not just the visible cyst. The surgeon takes the cyst, its track, the middle of the small U-shaped bone, and the track above the bone up toward the tongue base. This wide clearance is what keeps the lump from coming back.
steps.tx: The **Sistrunk procedure** (standard cyst operation) removes the cyst with its **tract** (duct channel), the central **hyoid bone** (neck U-bone), and the tract above the hyoid to the **tongue base** (channel origin). Taking the hyoid core with the suprahyoid tract in continuity is the step that secures cure.

steps.say: Cutting corners guarantees a second operation. Leaving any piece of the channel behind lets the cyst regrow in nearly half the cases. The forty to fifty percent recurrence after incomplete surgery is the strongest argument for doing the full clearance the first time. The scar and tongue base are watched for years after the operation.
steps.tx: Incomplete resection leaves recurrence in **40** (forty) to **50** (fifty) percent of cases. The **recurrence** (cyst regrowth) follows residual **thyroglossal tract** (duct remnant), so the hyoid core and suprahyoid channel must be taken in continuity at the first operation. Only **complete excision** (whole-tract removal) prevents regrowth. Follow up watches the scar and **tongue base** (tract origin) for years.

steps.say: Not every midline neck lump is a thyroglossal cyst. Firm nodules on the forehead, beside the eyebrow, over the soft spot or behind the ear are usually dermoid cysts holding skin parts like hair. A midline scalp lump needs a scan first to exclude a channel into the skull.
steps.tx: **Dermoid cysts** (skin-part lumps) of the forehead, lateral eyebrow, anterior **fontanelle** (soft spot) or postauricular skin contain **skin appendages** (hair and glands), while **epidermoid cysts** (flake-filled lumps) hold only epidermis and **keratin debris** (skin flakes). Midline scalp lesions need ultrasound to exclude a communicating **cephalocele** (brain-sac hernia). Most scalp lesions enlarge over time and erode bone (**osteolytic** change), and symptomatic nodules need **surgical excision** (operative removal).

steps.say: Swollen neck glands are common in children and most need no surgery. Glands that stay large, feel matted or sit above the collarbone earn a closer look with imaging for dead centres and a search for systemic disease. The picture shows how nodes cluster and drain across the neck triangles.
steps.tx: **Lymphadenopathy** (gland swelling) from viral illness needs observation alone, while fixed enlarging **supraclavicular nodes** (collarbone glands) with night sweats and weight loss raise **malignancy** (cancer) concern. Ultrasound detects **central necrosis** (dead gland centres) needing urgent surgery, and chest imaging hunts **mediastinal nodes** (chest glands).

steps.say: Operating in the front of the neck demands a map of what lies underneath. The big neck muscle, the great vein and the shoulder nerve crowd a small field, demanding a precise map. The dissection view shows these landmarks exactly as the surgeon meets them, orienting dissection.
steps.tx: Anterior neck surgery works around the **sternocleidomastoid** (strap muscle), the **internal jugular vein** (great neck vein), the **accessory nerve** (shoulder-muscle nerve) and gland chains. The lateral dissection view maps these **landmarks** (guide structures) so cyst tracts are cleared without injuring nerves or vessels.
